title: Resolution-standardized evaluation of ligand atomic coordinates in crystallographic structures using machine learning
summary: Accurate assessment of ligand coordinate-density consistency across different resolutions remains challenging in macromolecular crystallography. We introduce the atomic Box Correlation Coefficient (aBCC), an atom-level metric for evaluating the consistency between ligand atomic coordinates and electron density in a resolution-standardized framework. To predict aBCC values from electron-density maps, we developed QAEmap, a machine learning model based on three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D-CNNs). The model was trained using Fourier-truncated electron-density maps and corresponding ligand coordinates generated from high-resolution structures in the Protein Data Bank. It was evaluated using both Fourier-truncated electron-density maps and experimentally determined PDB structures. was evaluated using both Fourier-truncated electron-density maps and experimentally determined PDB structures.The prediction accuracy gradually decreased with decreasing resolution, but remained reliable up to ~3.5 angstrom. These results demonstrate that aBCC enables resolution-standardized atom-wise evaluation of coordinate-density consistency across different resolutions and provide a foundation for further development and refinement of machine learning-based coordinate validation.

title: Pyrenophora teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures to facilitate effector-driven promotion of in planta colonization on barley
summary: Pyrenophora teres f. teres is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes net form net blotch (NFNB) of barley. Infection of susceptible barley leaves initially causes dot-like lesions that progress to transverse and longitudinal striations, that form the net-like pattern of necrosis for which the disease was named. While the complex genetic architecture of the P. teres f. teres-barley interaction involves both dominant resistance and susceptibility and quantitative resistance, the in planta infection structures, compatible infection timeline, and the influence of effectors remain poorly defined. This study used fluorescent staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to define infection structures and characterize the compatible infection timeline of P. teres f. teres. Using CLSM in conjunction with image-segmentation machine learning, we generated a clear comparative infection timeline showing how P. teres f. teres isolates harboring zero, one, or two virulence effector alleles infect the barley cultivar Rika. We believe that the effector genes VR1 and VR2 contributed to virulence in a synergistic manner. The effector genes combined presence accelerated the timing and spread of programmed cell death, resulting in significantly greater hyphal volume and visibly more severe macroscopic lesion development. This suggests that P. teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures alongside effectors to maximize fungal colonization and hyphal positioning to optimize nutrient uptake, perpetuating its polycyclic life cycle.

title: Pili-like proteins are essential for conjugation also in Gram-positive bacteria
summary: Type IV secretion systems (T4SS) enable the spread of antibiotic resistance and other virulence factors. In Gram-positive bacteria, T4SSs have long been thought to lack VirB2-like proteins that form conjugative pili and instead rely on adhesins for cell-cell contacts. Yet, it has remained unclear how subsequent DNA transfer (conjugation) is mediated. Here we identify a VirB2-like protein, PrgFB2, from the clinically isolated plasmid pCF10 in Enterococcus faecalis and show that it is essential for conjugation. Structural modelling confidently predicts a pilus-like assembly for PrgFB2. This is in line with recently proposed models for conjugative pili in Gram-negative T4SSs. We validate the PrgFB2 pili prediction through mutagenesis, conjugation assays, and targeted chemical labelling. By combining various machine learning bioinformatic techniques, we analysed >1000 Gram-positive conjugative plasmids from diverse species, including major pathogens, and identified probable pili-forming VirB2-like proteins in a large majority. Our findings challenge the prevailing view that Gram-positive T4SSs lack pili and highlight critical targets for combating antimicrobial resistance and virulence in Gram-positive bacteria.

title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
summary: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

title: Koopman Analysis Reveals Collective Modes Governing Cellular Dynamics
summary: Living systems are complex nonlinear systems that operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and this nonlinearity makes their dynamics difficult to analyze. Several linearization techniques have been developed to address this problem, but most are local. Koopman operator theory is a powerful alternative that linearizes a system globally. Here we show that it not only achieves global linearization but also reveals collective modes that govern the dynamics of complex, out-of-equilibrium nonlinear systems. Applying the approach to whole-cell dynamical models, we find that these collective modes have physical and biological significance and relate to distinct processes in the cell cycle and in cell-state transitions. Collective and normal modes are widespread in many-body systems, particularly in condensed matter (e.g., magnons, phonons, hydrodynamic modes) and in macromolecular dynamics (e.g., normal mode analysis). By demonstrating that such modes also exist in cell-state transition dynamics, and in non-equilibrium nonlinear systems more generally, we offer a new theoretical-physics perspective on these systems. The collective modes separate into slow and fast modes. Long-term dynamics are governed by a few dominant slow modes that form a slow manifold of much lower dimension than the original state space. Thus, although the cell is a very high-dimensional system, its cell-cycle dynamics ultimately reduce to a low-dimensional space. Each mode comprises the coordinated behavior of groups of genes and reflects the structure of the underlying gene regulatory network. The modes can also be decomposed into terms that behave like damped harmonic oscillators, drawing an analogy between the modes of a nonlinear system and the normal modes of many-body systems. Finally, our analysis suggests that the dominant modes are closely associated with biological processes in the cell cycle, including mitosis, spindle checkpoint signaling, and DNA replication and repair.

title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
summary: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

title: Sodium coordination at the Na2 site enforces ion-substrate coupling in serotonin transporter SERT
summary: Secondary active transporters use the thermodynamically favorable movement of an ion down its electrochemical gradient to drive substrate accumulation against a concentration gradient. For the human serotonin transporter (SERT), strict coupling between Na and 5-HT transport is essential for maintaining neurotransmitter homeostasis, yet the structural mechanism by which Na binding enforces this coupling is incompletely understood. Here, we identify an interaction network through which Na coordination at the cation site Ct2 (also known as Na2) modulates conformational change on both sides of the transporter. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that Na occupancy of Ct2 stabilizes specific interactions between residues in TM5, TM8, and TM1 that together gate aqueous access to the cytoplasmic and extracellular pathways. Disruption of this network through mutations at Ct2 residues Asp437 and Ser438, or at the TM5 residue Thr284, reduces the concentrative power of SERT and allows a constitutive Na conductance, consistent with uncoupled Na uniport. These findings reveal how structural integrity at and around the Ct2 site enforces obligatory Na-5-HT coupling and thereby sustains the thermodynamic efficiency of serotonin uptake.

title: Biologically Guided Deep Learning for Personalized PSA Forecasting in Intermittent Prostate Cancer Therapy
summary: Intermittent Androgen Deprivation Therapy (IADT) offers a promising management strategy for prostate cancer by alternating treatment periods with the aim of delaying castration resistance and mitigating side effects. An evolutionary rationale for treatment interruptions is to preserve treatment-sensitive cells that may competitively suppress resistant populations. However, designing optimal patient-specific treatment schedules remains challenging due to the complex dynamics of tumor evolution and the computational intensity of traditional mechanistic simulation models. Standard mathematical models have prespecified structures that may inadequately capture patient-specific tumor evolution, limiting Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) forecasting accuracy and adaptation to new patient data. These limitations may reduce the effectiveness of treatment policies learned using these models. To address them, we present a domain-adapted machine learning framework that integrates biological constraints into the deep learning architecture and embeds historical biomarkers to act as a robust, computationally efficient neural surrogate for mechanistic simulations. This framework enhances generalization across sparse clinical profiles by leveraging deep neural representations for patient-specific and cross-patient parameter learning, and potentially enables the identification of personalized dosing schedules tailored to individual tumor trajectories. Preliminary evaluations confirm that it reliably captures treatment-associated PSA dynamics while overcoming the computational bottlenecks of numerical solvers. Ultimately, this work provides a scalable foundation for optimizing adaptive therapy protocols to extend time to disease progression. We present the architectural formulation, forecasting evaluation against mechanistic baselines, and training and optimization procedures of the deep neural networks.

title: Linking Early Bacterial Responses to Growth Inhibition via Glucose-Turbidity Dynamics for Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
summary: Earlier susceptibility information can guide timely antibiotic selection, while metabolic measurements can broaden the characterization of bacterial drug responses. We developed glucose-turbidity antimicrobial susceptibility testing (GT-AST) to pair residual-glucose assay signals with turbidity and relate early responses to growth inhibition. Among 43 cultured isolates, some antibiotic-exposed cultures showed glucose-associated changes despite attenuated turbidity responses. These observations provide physiological clues for studying metabolic activity when growth is limited, including future investigations of viable but non-culturable states or persister cells. Conventional broth microdilution relies on overnight growth readings; GT-AST used trajectories collected during approximately 2 h of antibiotic exposure to predict subsequent growth and estimate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Across 100 repeats of isolate-grouped cross-validation, essential agreement between predicted MICs and independently measured reference MICs averaged 87.1%. Eight bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimens were tested directly without prior bacterial isolation. Levofloxacin susceptibility classifications based on observed growth agreed with hospital results in all four culture-positive specimens. Exact and essential agreement between predicted and hospital MICs each averaged 99.0%. Together, these findings support developing GT-AST to provide earlier susceptibility information for effective, appropriately targeted treatment of patients. Keywords: antimicrobial susceptibility testing; glucose metabolism; turbidity; machine learning; minimum inhibitory concentration

title: BrainRoute integrates machine learning prediction with community-driven verification of blood-brain barrier permeability
summary: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective barrier that restricts the entry of many therapeutic agents into the brain. The lack of efficient methods for BBB permeability research and data management remains a significant challenge for central nervous system drug-development pipelines. Although BBB permeability data are available from multiple open sources, few platforms integrate these datasets with molecular exploration, predictive tools, and a structured process for community-supported data verification. Here, we present BrainRoute, an open platform for BBB molecular data collection, exploration, prediction, and community-supported verification. BrainRoute provides searchable and filterable molecular records, physicochemical and structural information, source-linked data, single-molecule and batch prediction, and a structured workflow through which users can submit additional evidence for review. The prediction tool model-development cohort contained 7,888 unique molecules, including 5,424 BBB+ and 2,464 BBB- molecules. Six machine-learning classifiers were evaluated using PaDEL descriptors, Morgan fingerprints, frozen ChemBERTa embeddings, and combined feature representations. The three selected models were integrated into the platform as a probability-averaged ensemble. The primary five-fold scaffold-grouped analysis achieved a best mean balanced accuracy of 0.783 {+/-} 0.026. On an independent external set containing 410 non-overlapping molecules, the deployed ensemble achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.659 (95% CI 0.600 - 0.712) and an AUPRC of 0.670 (95% CI 0.583 - 0.752). BrainRoute serves as a platform for exploring BBB-related molecular data and computational predictions while supporting the continued growth and verification of the underlying dataset. BrainRoute is freely accessible online (https://github.com/omicscodeathon/brainroutedb).

title: Phosphate selectivity in XPR1 is driven by direct multi-ion competition
summary: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) is essential for numerous cellular processes, and its intracellular concentration must be tightly regulated. In mammals, phosphate efflux is mediated by the Xenotropic and Polytropic Retrovirus Receptor 1 (XPR1/SLC53A1), the only known mammalian Pi exporter. We and others have recently proposed that XPR1 functions like a Pi channel, with the protein preferentially conducting the H2PO4- species of Pi over HPO42-. While some studies suggest that XPR1 can conduct other anions, the molecular basis of XPR1 substrate selectivity remains unknown. Here, we use over 110 s of molecular dynamics simulations, together with free-energy calculations, to investigate substrate selectivity in XPR1. We show that H2PO4- (Pi1-) is preferentially conducted over HPO42- (Pi2-), and that Pi1- progressively outcompetes Cl- for occupancy of the transport pathway. Free-energy and ion-interaction analyses reveal that selectivity arises from two distinct mechanisms: favourable protein-Pi interactions and direct ion-ion interactions in the pore. This direct contact facilitates Pi1- displacement via the previously proposed knock-kiss-kick mechanism, whereas entry of Cl- is restricted due to the preference for water-mediated interactions. Simulations with additional anions show that XPR1 remains permissive to several monovalent species, including nitrate, bicarbonate and methanesulfonate, while poorly conducting the divalent anion sulfate. These findings suggest that XPR1 does not achieve phosphate selectivity through absolute exclusion of competing anions. Instead, preferential Pi transport emerges from substrate-specific interactions and competition between multiple ions within a relatively permissive permeation pathway, providing a molecular basis for substrate discrimination in XPR1.

title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
summary: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

title: MDQ: A DockQ-Inspired Scoring Function for Assessing Interface Similarity and Clustering in Molecular Dynamics
summary: Assessing the similarity between protein-protein interfaces is essential for evaluating docking models, yet widely used metrics such as DockQ rely on a single native reference structure and yield asymmetric scores, making them unsuitable for molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories where no reference exists and frame-to-frame comparisons are required. Here, we introduce the MDQ, a fully symmetric reformulation of DockQ designed for MD trajectory analysis. MDQ replaces the fraction of native contacts with the Fraction of Shared Contacts (FSC), and redefines interface and ligand RMSD as weighted variants that penalize low atomic overlap between compared frames. The score can be used to follow structure/contacts convergence of an interface along a trajectory. And it is inverted to produce a true distance metric ranging from 0 (identical interfaces) to 1 (distinct interfaces), directly compatible with distance-based clustering. Applied to two benchmark complexes, Ail-Vitronectin and TGFBR1-FKBP12, MDQ heatmaps reveal global interface stability alongside subtle conformational rearrangements, while DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering of the MDQ distance matrix identifies representative conformational states. Then non-bonding interaction found in clusters were identified by MICLOT software. MDQ thus provides a robust and frame-to-frame symmetric framework for monitoring protein-protein interface conformational and interaction heterogeneity throughout MD simulations.

title: GPU handling of OPC water in GROMACS: validation by protein folding and a 1.6-fold speed-up
summary: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is one of the core computational methods of the life sciences, used to study protein folding, receptor activation and drug binding in atomic detail. The timescales it can reach depend on speed, and running each step entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU) is now essential for fast simulation. Optimal Point Charge (OPC) water, recommended for the ff19SB protein force field, carries its negative charge on a virtual site, and in GROMACS 2026.3 virtual sites prevent the coordinate update from running on the GPU. The GROMACS developers have recently added GPU handling of virtual sites to the development version as an experimental feature. Whether simulations run in this way agree with the established CPU calculation has to be measured, and no such test has been reported over microseconds or in a membrane-protein system of production size. We compared a modified build that handles OPC sites within the GPU update (Optimized) with the official release (Reference). The two builds placed the charge site with the same error (2.3 x 10^-7 nm) and gave relative force differences below 10^-6. In five matched pairs of 5-microsecond simulations, the Trp-cage miniprotein folded with both builds (three of five Reference and five of five Optimized runs; P = 0.44), and the folded ensembles matched. Both builds reproduced the density, diffusion coefficient, dielectric constant and second hydration shell that distinguish OPC from TIP3P water. In a 166,826-atom membrane system of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor, residue hydration agreed between the builds (r = 0.99), and Optimized ran 1.57-1.66 times as fast as tuned Reference on two GPUs, with 87-97% of the time saved coming from moving the coordinate update to the GPU. In these tests, GPU handling of OPC sites gave a substantial speed gain with no sign of altered physical behaviour.
